title: Why used cars are selling for new-car prices
dek: New-car price increases drag used cars up with them through the ‘price waterfall’, pandemic production cuts left the car market digesting for years like a snake swallowing a mouse, and US automakers simply stopped building cheap sedans — the cars you can get for $10,000 to $15,000 went from 5 years old to 9 years old.
why: One episode that lays out all three mechanisms behind expensive used cars, plus a counterintuitive place to find a deal: used EVs. Medium information density, but the conclusions are directly usable.
who: Anyone buying or replacing a car, investors watching US consumer and inflation data, and anyone doing business in autos or used-car finance.
skip: The show's opening and closing banter and ads, and the closing joke about a lime-green Cybertruck.

points.h: New-car price increases have actually stabilized
points.body: Many people assume the car market is still in runaway inflation, but the data doesn't say that. From 2019 to now, new-car prices rose 4.3% annualized, while overall CPI rose slightly under 4% annualized over the same period — the gap isn't outrageous. In other words, the new-car line has basically returned to the broader market's level. The real problem is the other half of the market: over the same period, used-car prices rose 5.5% annualized, beating both inflation and new cars. Today a used car just three years old averages over $32,000. So ‘cars are expensive’ is mainly not a new-car problem — it's a used-car problem.

points.h: Used-car prices follow new cars, and tariffs pass through too
points.body: The first mechanism is called the ‘price waterfall’: used-car prices follow new-car prices, and for the same brand and model, when the new-car price goes up or down, the used car moves with it. This isn't new. The key point is that even if a used car was built before tariffs took effect, its price is still affected by tariffs — because tariffs raise the cost of new cars and of the materials that go into building them, the whole water level of the waterfall rises, lifting the used cars downstream along with it. So hoping that ‘I'm buying an old car, tariffs have nothing to do with me’ doesn't hold up.

points.h: Pandemic production cuts are a snake swallowing a mouse, not yet digested
points.body: The second mechanism is supply. The drop in auto production in 2020 means that years later — say, 2026 — used-car buyers have fewer cars to choose from. Jeremy Robb's metaphor is ‘watching a snake swallow a mouse’: the low-production bottleneck propagates down the timeline, and when supply is thin, prices are generally high. The car market is that snake still slowly digesting the used-car mouse, and its stomach is still uncomfortable. This mechanism explains why, long after the pandemic, the selection of used cars is still narrow.

points.h: Automakers deliberately killed off cheap sedans
points.body: The third mechanism is a business decision, not an act of God. Ivan Drury says the automakers' judgment was ‘nobody wants sedans, so let's build more big SUVs’ — big SUVs sell for $60,000, $70,000, $80,000, even $100,000, while entry-level sedans at $20,000 to $30,000 were pushed out of the market entirely. US automakers have all but emptied out the whole category; Ford stopped building ordinary sedans like the Fiesta years ago; Japanese and Korean brands still have a few, German brands even fewer. The result is that an entire vehicle category has been compressed into a handful of choices, and anyone who wants ‘just a tool to get from A to B’ has to wait in line.

points.h: What $10,000 to $15,000 buys is four years older
points.body: Stack those three mechanisms together and the cheapest segment of the market has essentially been ‘scrapped’. Ivan Drury looked into that range: in 2019, $10,000 to $15,000 bought a car about 5 years old; today, the same money buys a car close to 9 years old with around 100,000 miles on it. This isn't just a change in numbers — it creates a personal-finance trap: trying to stay on budget invites more expenses instead. A car with 100,000 miles usually needs more repairs, and expensive, annoying parts like water pumps and timing belts fail, and people who can't fix cars themselves have to pay someone to do it. The money saved on the purchase price may flow right back out through repair bills.

points.h: Auto loan rates have doubled, but inflation data doesn't count them
points.body: There's another big cost that the statistical measure misses: interest. In 2019, a borrower with ‘good but not great’ credit could get a 4.5% auto loan rate; today the same person with the same loan faces a rate near 9%, roughly double. The key point is that the agencies that record inflation data only count the price of the car, not the monthly interest expense. So the official numbers don't look that bad, but the actual monthly payment burden on car buyers is much heavier. Ivan's advice is that you have to run the numbers yourself now: if you can get a very low APR on a new car, that low rate can completely erase the premise that ‘buying used is the better deal’.

points.h: Used EVs are the only corner still on sale
points.body: The car market isn't one single thing. Ivan Drury says there's one segment where you can still find a bargain: EVs. He describes EV resale values as ‘atrocious’, driven by misconceptions about EVs — how long the battery lasts, how reliable they are. Those misconceptions push used EV prices down, which in turn creates an opportunity for buyers, and he is bullish on this market. He acknowledges that the technology really is iterating fast, which makes people feel that ‘buy today and it's obsolete tomorrow’, but for many cars, even once the tech is outdated, it still works fine functionally.
